blocks.title: Seismometer
blocks.text: A seismometer is an instrument that responds to any movement of the rocks under the ground, or vibration caused by earthquakes, volcanic eruptions and explosions. It detects earthquakes by using electromagnetic induction to convert ground motion into electrical signals.

Typically a seismometer includes a weight suspended by a spring. When an earthquake occurs, the ground moves but the weight tends to stay stationary because of its inertia. This results in relative motion between the weight and the frame of the seismometer, which is attached to the ground. The weight is often attached to a magnet which moves inside a coil of wire (Fig. 10.19). This set-up works according to Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction: the changing magnetic flux through the coil induces an emf in the coil, which gives rise to an induced electric current.

The induced current is proportional to the velocity of the ground motion. The electrical signals generated are amplified and recorded, providing data on the amplitude, frequency and duration of the earthquake waves. The data are analysed to determine various characteristics of the earthquake, such as its location, magnitude and depth.

Usually a seismometer is buried under the ground at a depth of 50 to 1000 metres, in a protective case called a vault: a cylindrical steel tank approximately 1 metre wide and 2 metres deep, with a concrete pad at the bottom (Fig. 10.20). In the station of Fig. 10.20, solar energy charges the batteries, GPS gives the location, the seismic equipment in the vault transmits data, and a computer stores the data.

Most earthquakes are caused by plate tectonics (displacement). The book classes those down to about 60 km deep as shallow, intermediate ones as deep as 280 km beneath the crust, and deep earthquakes as reaching depths past 280 km (For Your Information). There are two main types of seismic waves: P-waves, the primary waves, which are longitudinal, and S-waves, the secondary waves, which are transverse in nature (For Your Information).

blocks.prompt: A magnet hangs from a spring and oscillates in and out of a coil connected to a galvanometer. What does the galvanometer show (MCQ 10.10)? What would you do to protect a sensitive instrument from stray magnetic fields (constructed response 10.9)?
blocks.explanation: As the magnet moves in, the flux through the coil increases, and as it moves out the flux decreases, so the galvanometer swings to the left and to the right; by Lenz's law the induced currents oppose the motion and take energy from it, so the oscillation and the deflection die away: option (d). Enclose the instrument in a box of soft iron or another high-permeability material, which carries the external field lines round the inside so that the field within the box is very small.

items: Seismometer: a magnet on a spring inside a coil on the frame; the ground and coil move, the magnet stays still by inertia, the changing flux induces an emf (Faraday's law); the induced current is proportional to the ground velocity; amplified and recorded to give location, magnitude and depth.
Buried 50 to 1000 m in a vault (steel tank about 1 m by 2 m); P-waves longitudinal, S-waves transverse; most earthquakes come from plate tectonics.
